analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to tell customers the overdraft fee amount and get their consent before charging it.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Financial Services Committee and died when the Congress ended, having attracted no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred banks from charging an overdraft fee — the charge for spending more than your checking account holds — unless the bank first told the customer, in plain terms, that the transaction would trigger an overdraft and how much the fee would be, and let the customer accept or decline. It applied to ATM withdrawals, debit card purchases at stores, in-person and phone transactions, and online banking. It also required monthly statements to show what interest rate each overdraft fee amounts to on the money borrowed.
analysis.who_benefits: Checking account customers, especially those who run low balances and get hit with a fee of around $35 for a single small transaction. The bill would have let them see the fee before the transaction went through and choose to cancel instead — for example, an ATM screen would have shown the overdraft amount and fee with ACCEPT and DECLINE buttons [S3]. Monthly statements would have shown each fee as an annual percentage rate, making clear how expensive a $35 fee on a $40 shortfall really is [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Checking account customers hit with overdraft fees

how_it_helps.text: No overdraft fee could be charged unless the bank notified the customer before the transaction completed, for in-person, ATM, phone, and internet transactions [S2].
ATM and store terminal screens would have displayed the overdraft amount and the fee, with buttons to accept or cancel the transaction [S3].
Monthly statements would have to state the annual percentage rate each overdraft fee represents on the overdraft amount [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other financial institutions that collect overdraft fees would have lost some of that fee income, since customers shown the fee upfront could decline and some banks would have faced costs to reprogram ATMs, point-of-sale terminals, and statements.

drawbacks.text: The bill only required notice and consent, not fee caps — a customer who accepted could still be charged a large fee for a small overdraft, so the underlying charge remained untouched [S2].

Requiring an accept-or-decline screen on every ATM and store terminal that would overdraw an account adds a step to transactions and imposes compliance and reprogramming costs on banks and terminal operators [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to customers is straightforward and the cost to banks is real but modest: overdraft fees are a large revenue line for banks charged mainly to customers with thin balances, and showing people the fee before it lands is a modest consumer protection, not a ban on fees. Its main weakness is that it notifies rather than restricts — fees could still be steep once accepted.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kendrick Meek of Florida introduced the bill on March 12, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1].
The committee took no further action after the referral; there was no markup, no floor vote, and no further action listed for the remainder of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks that collect overdraft fees came out ahead, because no pre-transaction notice requirement was enacted and fee income continued. Checking account customers who pay overdraft fees lost the chance for advance notice and a decline option.

for.name: Rep. Kendrick Meek
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it sat after referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, and no recorded votes show where members stood.

industries.industry: Banks and other deposit-taking financial institutions
industries.note: Overdraft fees are a major fee-income source for banks, charged to account holders who overdraw. Requiring upfront notice and an accept-or-decline choice would have let many customers avoid the fee, cutting that revenue; the industry's interest in the bill ran against the customers paying the fees.
